title: Numbers, Time & Money
description: Counting, prices in ribu and juta, telling the time, days and dates, and the money talk of paying at a stall: how much, change and the exact amount.

phrases.registerNotes: Every vowel keeps its sound, except the e in empat, which is a quick, neutral 'uh': uhm-pat.
Sepuluh is se- (one) plus puluh (ten). The same se- gives seratus (100) and seribu (1,000).
phrases.pitfallNote: Enam, delapan, sembilan and sepuluh all start with that quick 'uh': uh-nam, duh-la-pan, suhm-bi-lan, suh-pu-luh.

phrases.indonesian: sebelas, dua belas, dua puluh, dua puluh satu
phrases.registerNotes: Belas makes the teens (tiga belas, 13) and puluh the tens (tiga puluh, 30). After that you just add: dua puluh lima is 25.

phrases.indonesian: seratus, seribu, sepuluh ribu, seratus ribu
phrases.registerNotes: Ratus is hundred and ribu thousand. Most prices you'll pay are in ribu, and the notes in your wallet run from one thousand to a hundred thousand.
phrases.pitfallNote: One hundred and one thousand take se-: seribu, not satu ribu; seratus, not satu ratus.

phrases.registerNotes: Point at what you mean. Harganya is 'its price'; Berapa, Bu? is the short everyday version.
Prices are said in thousands, and rupiah is usually left off. At a market you may hear just dua puluh lima, with the ribu understood.
phrases.pitfallNote: Written, it's Rp25.000: Indonesian groups thousands with a full stop and uses a comma for decimals, the other way round from English.

phrases.registerNotes: Juta is million: rent, flights and phones are priced in juta. Setengah (half) works the same way in any price: dua setengah juta is 2.5 million.
At the end, at a warung or a stall, to ask for the total. Jadi berapa? (So how much?) is just as common.

phrases.indonesian: Maaf, uangnya seratus ribu. Ada kembalian?
phrases.english: Sorry, I've only got a hundred thousand. Have you got change?
phrases.registerNotes: Kembalian is change. Small stalls and drivers often can't break a big note, and may ask you Ada uang kecil? (Anything smaller?).
phrases.cultureNote: Keep small notes for warungs, ojeks and parking attendants; starting with maaf acknowledges the nuisance of a big note.

phrases.registerNotes: Say it as you hand over the exact amount. Staff may ask Ada uang pas? (Have you got the exact money?).
Market fruit and vegetables are sold by weight: sekilo (a kilo), setengah kilo, seperempat kilo (a quarter).
Jam berapa? on its own works too. With a stranger, start with Maaf or Permisi.
phrases.pitfallNote: Word order matters: jam berapa is what time, berapa jam is how many hours.

phrases.registerNotes: Pukul tiga is the formal version, used on the news and in writing.
phrases.pitfallNote: Jam tiga is three o'clock; tiga jam is three hours.

phrases.registerNotes: Jam goes first for clock times: jam tiga (three o’clock), jam setengah empat (half past three).
phrases.pitfallNote: Setengah empat means halfway to four, so 3:30, not 4:30. English speakers get this wrong and turn up an hour late.

phrases.registerNotes: Kurang (less) is 'to' and lewat is 'past': jam sembilan lewat sepuluh is ten past nine. Many people just say the minutes: jam delapan empat puluh lima.
There's no a.m. or p.m.: add pagi, siang, sore or malam. Timetables use the 24-hour clock, written 19.00.

phrases.english: What time do you open tomorrow?
phrases.registerNotes: Buka is open and tutup is closed: Tutup jam berapa? (What time do you close?). Hari ini (today) and besok (tomorrow) can go first or last.
The answer: Hari ini hari Jumat. Hari (day) goes before the day's name: hari Senin, on Monday.
Day names take a capital letter, and usually hari before them in a sentence: Sampai hari Kamis (See you Thursday).
Days are usually said with hari: hari Jumat, hari Sabtu. On a sign or a timetable they appear on their own.
phrases.pitfallNote: Minggu is also 'week': hari Minggu is Sunday, but minggu depan is next week.
phrases.cultureNote: Muslim men go to midday prayers on Friday, so some offices and services stop for a long lunch on Jumat.

phrases.registerNotes: Tanggal is the date: Hari ini tanggal lima. Dates go day, month, year, as in New Zealand.
phrases.cultureNote: Tujuh belas Agustus, 17 August, is Independence Day; neighbourhoods hold games and races for it, called tujuh belasan.

phrases.registerNotes: What staff ask at a restaurant door or a ticket counter. Answer Dua orang (two people), or just Berdua.
phrases.pitfallNote: Berapa is both how many and how much, and the thing counted follows it: berapa orang, berapa hari.

phrases.registerNotes: Ber- plus a number means 'as a group of': berdua (the two of us), bertiga, berempat, berlima. Empat orang (four people) also works.

phrases.indonesian: Umur saya tiga puluh dua tahun.
phrases.registerNotes: The question is Umurnya berapa? or, to someone older, Umur Bapak berapa? Tahun (years) is often left off.
phrases.cultureNote: Age comes up early because it decides how people address each other: Kak or Adik, Mas or Pak.

phrases.english: Can I have your WhatsApp number?
phrases.registerNotes: WA (said 'we a') is WhatsApp, how almost everyone keeps in touch. Phone numbers are read one digit at a time, with nol or kosong for zero.
